title: Another pdh bites the dust
clues: A thin red groove and petechial spots on Prof Aishik’s neck indicate strangulation rather than a fall.
A length of utility rope with frayed fibers is found partly hidden behind the office cabinet baseboard.
The office chair is toppled and the desk lamp is knocked sideways, consistent with a struggle.
Fresh powdery chalk/white dust is smeared on the office door handle, matching common lab board chalk.
Yeet admits to a budget-cut argument but has a documented lab log-in during the presumed time of death.
Kuluhan Binici keeps spare rope for bundling trash bags, but his rope is a different weave and stored intact.
Prof Aishik’s keyboard shows a clear set of fresh fingerprints on the right side near the Enter key.
The fingerprint set matches Taha Aksu, and Taha’s claim he has never used that keyboard becomes false.
A hidden folder labeled “Qualifying—Rubric & Past Questions” is missing from the bottom drawer dividers.
A faint rope-burn mark on Taha’s inner wrist aligns with a tight loop being pulled under strain.
Security desk logs show only one after-hours office entry badge event besides Prof Aishik’s: Taha’s temporary access.
items: Kuluhan Binici’s cleaning cart rope bundle
text:
Another pdh bites the dust

The summer term had hollowed out NUS SOC3. The lobby lights were on, but the couches looked freshly vacuumed and unused; the only footsteps belonged to graduate students slipping between labs and the pantry with coffee, like ghosts with deadlines. Detective Lim Wei Jian signed in at the security desk and followed Dr Siti Rahman, the faculty manager, up to Level 3.

The corridor outside Prof Aishik’s office smelled faintly of lemon disinfectant. A single strip light flickered near the stairwell, casting a stuttering shadow over a toppled “Research Seminar” poster stand. Two officers waited by the door, careful not to touch the handle.

Phase 1 — Objective: Establish cause of death via examining the body (Low)

Inside, Prof Aishik’s office was a cramped box of academia: two overfilled bookcases, framed conference badges, a whiteboard scrawled with committee tasks, and a desk that faced the windowless wall. The air-conditioning was cold enough to raise goosebumps.

Prof Aishik lay half-seated against the side of his desk as if he had tried to crawl away. His chair was on its side, one wheel still turning. The desk lamp lay knocked over, its metal shade dented.

Lim crouched, not touching, and studied the neck. There was a thin, angry red groove running around it—too neat, too complete to be a collar mark. Under the jawline, tiny pinprick spots dotted the skin, and the face carried a congested, grim set that didn’t match a simple collapse.

“People said he fell,” Dr Siti murmured, voice tight. “He was found like this in the morning. The first guess was—”

“A fall would leave impact bruising, maybe a head wound,” Lim said. He nodded at the lamp, the scuffed carpet, the scattered papers. “This is a struggle. And that groove—rope or cord.”

One officer leaned closer with a flashlight. At the base of the neck, fibers clung near the groove: pale strands, almost like synthetic thread.

Lim’s objective was simple: confirm the cause. He photographed the marks, noted the petechiae, and asked for the on-call pathologist to prioritize strangulation indicators.

Then he looked for what strangled him.

The office was small enough that every item mattered. Lim traced the edges of the room with his eyes: the cabinet tucked beside the door, the waste bin, a stack of printed exam schedules on a side table. Near the cabinet baseboard, something pale peeked out from shadow.

He had gloves pulled on before he knelt and gently pulled.

A length of utility rope slid free—thin, off-white, with frayed fibers and a faint kink as if it had been looped and yanked tight.

Dr Siti’s breath caught. “That wasn’t— that shouldn’t be there.”

Lim sealed it in an evidence bag. The twist was now certainty: Prof Aishik hadn’t died from a fall. He had been strangled with a rope.

Phase 2 — Objective: Locate the hidden evidence in the office (Medium)

Lim’s second objective was harder: why had someone come here, after-hours, in an almost-empty building, and fought the department head?

He started with what the office showed. The bottom drawer of the desk was shut but slightly misaligned, as if slammed in haste. Lim opened it carefully. Inside were files arranged with obsessive neatness—except for a set of cardboard dividers at the very back, where one slot was empty, the remaining tabs bent as if something had been hastily pulled out.

The empty tab label still read: “Qualifying—Rubric & Past Questions.”

“Prof Aishik kept old qualifying materials?” Lim asked.

Dr Siti nodded. “Locked drawer, normally. For committee reference. He was strict about it.”

The drawer lock plate showed a faint scrape, as if a key had been forced in and twisted quickly—or the right key used in a hurry.

Lim moved to the desk. Prof Aishik’s keyboard sat slightly skewed, as though shoved aside. He had a technician dust it. The powder settled in clear ridges of print on the right side—near Enter, where someone might brace a hand while using the mouse with the other.

“Fresh,” the technician said. “Not smeared with old oils. Someone used it recently.”

Lim had suspects ready before he left the room.

He walked down the corridor to the SOC3 lab room, where the hum of machines replaced the office’s dead silence. Inside, Yeet sat at a bench, surrounded by labeled sample containers and a whiteboard filled with budget numbers crossed out in frustration. The air smelled of solder and instant noodles.

Yeet looked up, eyes ringed with sleeplessness. “I know why you’re here,” Yeet said. “We fought about lab funding last week. He cut us again. I shouted. Everyone heard.”

Lim’s objective in this scene was to test motive against opportunity. “Where were you last night after 10?”

Yeet pushed a laptop toward Lim. “Logged into the lab server at 10:07. Ran a job till after midnight. The system logs are there. Ask anyone—this run was overdue.”

On the lab bench, a small block of white chalk sat by a board marker, dusting the bench with powder.

Lim noted it, then checked the lab attendance log pinned to a corkboard. Yeet’s name was on it with time stamps.

“Your argument matters,” Lim said, “but logs matter too.”

Next, he went to the cleaning room—an unglamorous nook that smelled of wet mop heads and detergent. Kuluhan Binici stood by a cart as if he’d been born leaning on it, arms crossed. He was grizzled, unimpressed, and exactly as grumpy as Dr Siti had warned.

“You think I did it,” Kuluhan said, before Lim could speak. “Because I’m the cleaner.”

Lim’s objective here was to match the rope. “Do you keep rope?”

Kuluhan jerked a thumb at a bundle on the cart. “For trash bags. Tie them. So they don’t spill everywhere because some students can’t aim.”

Lim examined it without touching. The rope on the cart was thicker, a different weave—more braided, less frayed. It was intact, tied in a neat coil.

“Anyone else take supplies?” Lim asked.

Kuluhan snorted. “New kids take anything. They don’t ask. They just—” He waved a hand. “The new PhD. Taha Aksu. Always in a rush. Always polite. Too polite. He asked for ‘spare string’ once. I told him find his own.”

Lim filed that away and walked to the pantry, which overlooked the empty courtyard through tall glass. A single graduate student sat there, headphones on, oblivious. Lim used the quiet to connect two earlier details: the chalk dust he’d seen in the lab, and the faint powder smear he remembered on Prof Aishik’s office door handle—white, fine, like someone who’d been writing on a board and then grabbed the handle.

He returned to the security desk. The guard pulled up keycard events: after-hours entries to the Level 3 office corridor. Prof Aishik’s card registered once in the evening. Another badge registered later, close to midnight.

Name on the badge: Taha Aksu—temporary access.

Only one new PhD student matched that.

Lim found Taha Aksu in the SOC3 Building itself, in a small graduate study space off the corridor: a room of empty desks, abandoned project posters, and one humming standing fan. Taha sat alone with a laptop open to a slide deck labeled “Qualifying Prep.” His posture was straight, his expression carefully neutral.

Lim’s objective now was to pin down the office evidence and the missing folder.

“Taha,” Lim said, “you had access to Prof Aishik’s office.”

Taha swallowed. “He gave me temporary access. For onboarding. I didn’t— I didn’t use it last night.”

Lim placed the printed keycard log on the table between them. The fan clicked as it oscillated, and outside the corridor lights buzzed in summer emptiness.

Taha’s eyes flicked once to the time stamp and away. “Someone could have—”

“Your badge, your entry,” Lim said. “And we found fresh fingerprints on Prof Aishik’s keyboard. If you never used it, you can explain why your prints are on the right side near Enter.”

Taha’s mouth opened, then closed.

Lim continued, carefully. “A folder is missing from his drawer: qualifying rubric and past questions. You’re new. You’re ambitious. You’re facing a qualifying exam.”

Taha’s fingers tightened around his phone. On his inner wrist, just above the watch line, Lim saw a faint abrasion—a narrow, reddish band, as if something had cinched down under strain.

“You were there to steal that folder,” Lim said. “You grabbed the handle with chalk on your hands—your lab chalk. You opened the drawer, pulled the file. Prof Aishik caught you. The struggle knocked his chair, his lamp. You panicked.”

Taha’s eyes glistened with anger or fear—hard to tell. “He was going to fail me,” Taha whispered. “He said it would ‘build character.’ He said I didn’t deserve—”

“He caught you in his office,” Lim said, voice steady. “You used a utility rope—something easy to grab, easy to hide behind a cabinet. You strangled him to silence him. Then you tried to make it look like a fall.”

Taha shook his head too fast. “No. No—”

The technician’s report arrived on Lim’s phone as a message from forensics: the lifted prints from the keyboard matched Taha Aksu.

Lim stood. “This building is empty in summer, Taha. That’s why you thought you’d get away with it. But emptiness preserves details: a rope hidden poorly, a missing folder tab left bent, a powder smear on a handle, and fingerprints on a keyboard you claim you never touched.”

Taha’s shoulders slumped. The fan kept clicking. Somewhere down the corridor, a graduate student’s laughter echoed briefly, then died.

When Lim signaled the officers, Taha finally spoke, voice cracked and small. “I just needed to pass.”

Lim watched the handcuffs close. The case was no longer a rumor about a fall, no longer an office accident whispered about in an empty summer campus.

It was murder—and the culprit was Taha Aksu.
